content: The actions of omega-3 (ω-3) and omega-6 (ω-6) essential fatty acids (EFAs) are best understood through their interactions, as they cannot be fully comprehended in isolation. Arachidonic acid (AA), a 20-carbon ω-6 fatty acid, is a key player in the arachidonic acid cascade, which encompasses over 20 signaling pathways that regulate numerous physiological functions, particularly those related to inflammation and the central nervous system (CNS). Most AA in the human body originates from dietary linoleic acid (18:2 ω-6), an essential fatty acid found in vegetable oils and animal fats. In the inflammatory response, two other groups of dietary EFAs form cascades that parallel and compete with the arachidonic acid cascade. Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5 ω-3) generates the most significant competing cascade, while dihomo-γ-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3 ω-6) forms a third, less prominent cascade. These parallel cascades mitigate the inflammatory effects of AA and its derivatives. A diet low in these less inflammatory EFAs, particularly ω-3s, is associated with various inflammation-related diseases. Modern diets in industrialized countries contain significantly less ω-3 fatty acids compared to diets from a century ago, which themselves had less ω-3 than the diets of early hunter-gatherers. The altered ω-3 to ω-6 ratio in contemporary diets has coincided with increased rates of inflammation-related diseases, often referred to as diseases of civilization. Strong evidence now supports the role of increased dietary ω-3 in alleviating several of these diseases, with preliminary evidence suggesting benefits for certain psychiatric disorders as well. Eicosanoids, signaling molecules derived from EFAs, are a major pathway through which EFAs exert their effects in the body. There are four classes of eicosanoids, each with two or three series. These molecules are synthesized from 20-carbon polyunsaturated EFAs, such as AA, EPA, or DGLA, which are cleaved from cell membrane phospholipids in response to inflammatory signals. The EFAs are then oxygenated via cyclooxygenase (COX) or lipoxygenase pathways, leading to the production of eicosanoids. COX oxidation removes two double bonds, producing thromboxanes (TX), prostaglandins (PG), and prostacyclins (PGI), while lipoxygenase oxidation retains the double bonds, forming leukotrienes (LK). The resulting eicosanoids are further modified into specific series, characterized by the number of double bonds they retain. The arachidonic acid cascade begins with the conversion of dietary linoleic acid (18:2 ω-6) into AA, which is then incorporated into cell membrane phospholipids. In response to inflammatory stimuli, phospholipase enzymes release AA as a free fatty acid. AA can then be oxygenated and modified to form eicosanoids, which act as autocrine and paracrine agents, binding to receptors on the same or neighboring cells. Alternatively, AA can diffuse into the cell nucleus and interact with transcription factors to regulate the expression of cytokines or other hormones. Eicosanoids derived from AA generally promote inflammation, while those from DGLA (via GLA) and EPA are less inflammatory, inactive, or even anti-inflammatory. For example, dietary ω-3 and GLA counteract the inflammatory effects of AA-derived eicosanoids through three mechanisms: displacement, competitive inhibition, and direct counteraction. 1. Displacement: Dietary ω-3 reduces tissue concentrations of AA. Animal studies show that increased dietary ω-3 leads to decreased AA levels in the brain and other tissues. Linolenic acid (18:3 ω-3) displaces linoleic acid (18:2 ω-6) from the elongase and desaturase enzymes that produce AA. EPA also inhibits phospholipase A2, reducing the release of AA from cell membranes. 2. Competitive Inhibition: DGLA and EPA compete with AA for access to COX and lipoxygenase enzymes, reducing the production of AA-derived eicosanoids. For instance, dietary GLA increases tissue DGLA and lowers thromboxane B2 (TXB2) levels. Similarly, EPA inhibits the production of series-2 prostaglandins (PG) and thromboxanes (TX). 3. Direct Counteraction: Some eicosanoids derived from DGLA and EPA directly counteract their AA-derived counterparts. For example, DGLA produces PGE1, which strongly opposes the effects of PGE2. EPA generates prostacyclin PGI3, an anti-aggregatory agent, and leukotriene LTB5, which counteracts the pro-inflammatory actions of AA-derived LTB4. The paradox of dietary GLA lies in its anti-inflammatory properties, despite being derived from linoleic acid (LA, 18:2 ω-6), which is pro-inflammatory. Unlike LA, GLA does not compete for the Δ6-desaturase enzyme, allowing its elongation product, DGLA, to inhibit inflammation through competitive inhibition and direct counteraction. Dietary GLA significantly increases DGLA levels in white blood cell membranes, whereas LA does not. Eicosanoid signaling pathways are highly complex, making it challenging to characterize the actions of individual eicosanoids. For example, PGE2 binds to four distinct receptors (EP1–EP4), each encoded by separate genes and existing in multiple isoforms. These receptors couple to different G proteins, leading to varying intracellular effects. EP2 and EP4 receptors, along with one EP3 isoform, couple to Gs proteins, increasing intracellular cAMP and exerting anti-inflammatory effects. In contrast, EP1 and other EP3 isoforms couple to Gq proteins, increasing intracellular calcium and promoting inflammation. Another EP3 isoform couples to Gi proteins, which decrease cAMP and increase calcium. Immune cells often express multiple receptors that activate opposing pathways, adding further complexity. EPA-derived PGE3 likely has distinct effects on this system, but these are not well-characterized. In the central nervous system (CNS), the arachidonic acid cascade operates differently. Neurohormones, neuromodulators, or neurotransmitters act as first messengers, activating phospholipase enzymes to release AA from neuron cell membranes. Free AA can influence ion channels and protein kinases within neurons or be metabolized into eicosanoids, epoxy-eicosatrienoic acids (EETs), neuroprotectin D, or endocannabinoids like anandamide. The roles of eicosanoids in the brain are less understood than their roles in inflammation, but they are thought to act as second messengers within neurons, regulating presynaptic inhibition and protein kinase C activation. They may also function as paracrine mediators, synchronizing the activity of interconnected neural cells. During development and certain forms of learning, postsynaptic cells may secrete regulatory factors that influence presynaptic terminals, a phenomenon known as retrograde regulation. Arachidonic acid metabolites are proposed to play a role in retrograde signaling and other forms of local neuronal activity modulation. The EPA and DGLA cascades are also present in the brain, and their eicosanoid metabolites have been detected. However, their specific effects on mental and neural processes are not as well-characterized as their roles in inflammation. Further research is needed to elucidate these mechanisms.
